prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at once without a lattice light shift, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the optical lattice clock (Katori and Ye) as my single-part position. Nothing in round 1 disputed that the science is real, that it has been reproduced by several independent laboratories at the 10^-18 level, or that the attribution of the core idea is unusually clean. The central point is that the discovery is a principle, not only an improvement in accuracy: a trapping field tuned to a magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift of the clock transition, so that a large number of neutral atoms can be held free of Doppler and recoil effects and interrogated in parallel. That is what moved the field beyond the single-ion limit, and it is separate from the frequency comb (counting optical cycles) and from ion control (the 2012 prize). On the chair's priority question, as I recall it and subject to a check against the record: Katori's group published the magic-wavelength lattice proposal around 2001-2003 and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock around 2003 and onward; Lemonde and Wolf published a shallow-lattice proposal and analysis in 2005, after it, and Ye's group realised the accuracy and stability frontier and later the many-body regime. That ordering supports a Katori-Ye pair, with Lemonde a legitimate but later contributor. On the redefinition of the second, I think the pending decision is a metrology-body milestone and not a scientific criterion, and the prize criterion is already met by what has been demonstrated: clocks agreeing across laboratories, millimetre-scale redshift measurements and constraints on drifts of constants. I would act now and not wait.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, the lattice clock sits in a lineage with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and a committee member could fairly read it as a continuation. I think this is answered by the citation, which must rest on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and not on frequency measurement in general, but the answer depends on drafting. Second, it is a narrower field than moire matter or topological phases, as Danielsson, Mehlig and Pearce say, and part of its broader impact (a new definition of the second, geodesy) is still prospective. Third, two names leave out Lemonde, other clock groups and the theorists of the magic-wavelength shifts, and my own account of the priority history is from memory. Finally, my judgement is shaped by being an atomic and optical physicist, and I may overvalue precision measurement relative to a discovery that opens a new class of phenomena.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I see the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait or to act now, and argued that the prize would reward capability more than a completed discovery.
responses.response: I would act now. The redefinition depends on a decision by the metrology community and on consistency of comparisons between clocks and the existing caesium realisation, and those are schedule matters, not tests of whether the lattice clock works. What a prize rests on is already in hand: independent clocks agreeing at the 10^-18 level, redshift measured over millimetres, and limits on variation of constants. I accept that this is a capability as well as a discovery, but the conceptual step, cancelling the light shift of a trapped neutral-atom ensemble, is a discovery in the sense of the statutes and not merely an engineering gain. If the committee thinks the redefinition should come first, that is an argument about timing in a later year and does not change my reading of the science.

responses.point: Lindroth argued that the comb solved counting optical cycles whereas the lattice clock solved holding a large ensemble without perturbing the transition, so the citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and not read as a second comb prize.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my citation accordingly: it now names the invention of the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, and refers to the 10^-18 level only as development. I would add one caution from my own side. Ye's comb background is why the stability frontier was reached so quickly, and a skeptical colleague will say so, so the citation should not lean on the stability as such. I also take your point that the earlier prizes cover the comb and single-ion control, not neutral-atom lattices, so I do not regard novelty as the weakest part of the case, though I now state it as the most contestable one.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B047 first on the breadth of what it opened, said a lattice clock is an extraordinary measurement improvement while moire materials changed the questions a community can ask, and called B019 a respectable outcome.
responses.response: The breadth argument is the strongest one against my position and I do not dismiss it. Where I differ is on how to weigh breadth against what is settled. Moire matter has opened a large field, but what is settled is the existence of flat-band-driven correlated phases, whereas the lattice clock's whole claim is settled and keeps being reproduced. Also, a clock has opened questions as well: it turns gravitational redshift, dark-matter coupling and constant drifts into laboratory measurements, and the many-body regime of interrogated atoms is a new physical question. I still read this as narrower, and I accept that.

responses.point: Mehlig said B019 has the cleanest attribution and he would not oppose it, but its reach in new phenomena is narrower than moire matter, calling it a strong candidate for a later year or a plausible partner part of a two-part prize.
responses.response: I considered the two-part idea seriously, since the chair asked for it. I decided against pairing B019 with B047 or B012 because the combination would put four to six credited names into a single prize, with a cap of three people overall, forcing me to cut either Katori or Ye or an essential name from the other part. A configuration that splits a clean pair to make room for a different field would answer a counting problem and not a scientific one. I also do not see why it should wait: the scientific case does not improve with the redefinition, and the principle has already been confirmed for two decades. I agree that the citation should not claim broad new phenomena.

responses.point: Olsson, who prefers B047 and keeps B019 as an alternative, said that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes weakens novelty, and disagreed with ranking B047 low on maturity alone, since replication across many groups is exactly the confirmation the clock community cites.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge and I concede part of it. Replication of the correlated insulating and superconducting states across many groups does show they are real, and I no longer treat the open superconducting mechanism as disqualifying in itself; the criterion is a discovery, not a finished explanation. My remaining worry is narrower: twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison with theory, and the credit around the 2018 experiments is concentrated, so I would put B047 as my second alternative, not at the bottom, and I would support it in a later year or if the committee prefers it. On overlap, the comb and ion-control prizes did not cover magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which is why I keep the novelty case.

responses.point: Johansson said B019 is the strongest non-topological option but that its full recognition may come with the redefinition of the second, and that a metrology advance sits in the lineage of the comb prize.
responses.response: Thank you for deferring on the systematics; I think the systematic budgets are in good shape, since comparisons between independent clocks at the 10^-18 level are the check. On the redefinition I disagree with the timing, as I wrote to Pearce. On B004 I have now dropped it as an alternative: the 2025 prize, the unresolved Devoret-Girvin-Koch credit and your own recusal advice all weigh against it, and I do not want to carry a candidate for which no member currently advocates.

responses.point: Eriksson holds DMFT first with reduced certainty and concedes that the attribution objection cannot be fully answered, saying that if no fair three-name prize exists the committee should look elsewhere on the shortlist.
responses.response: I appreciate that candour and I think it points to the right test for every candidate, including mine. The test for B005 is whether a fair three-person list exists, and Metzner, Muller-Hartmann and Jarrell make that hard; I do not think Vollhardt, Georges and Kotliar can be defended against that omission. I also still doubt that a framework is a discovery in the statutory sense, though your point about spectroscopy and Mott-transition thermodynamics shows it can be tested. By the same test, a Katori-Ye pair is defensible because I know of no one else whose contribution to the core idea has to be left out, and I have tried to say where I am not certain.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; this depends on how the citation is worded.

The priority history among Katori's 2001-2003 proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, Lemonde and Wolf's 2005 work and Ye's group's early realisations, which I recall from memory and which should be checked against the record before the citation is fixed.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should count as a reason to wait; I think not, but others judge differently.
Whether my atomic-physics background leads me to undervalue the breadth argument for B047 and the maturity-plus-breadth argument for B012, and whether B012 can be given a fair three-name citation.
statement.conflict_note: I repeat my disclosure from round 1. My profile records a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is the mentor of Jun Ye, one of the proposed laureates, so there is an indirect scientific connection to B019; I would accept a recusal discussion on that part. Nothing documented in my profile is a direct personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. My Lund ties, including quantum-memory collaborations and WACQT, bear on B004 and B017, which I have dropped from my alternatives. I note no further conflict for B012 or B047.
